title: Lesson 33: Bulkification & Trigger Frameworks: Limits-Aware Design That Scales
description: Why a trigger that works on one record fails on a data load, and how bulkification plus a trigger framework keep every layer working on collections under the governor ceiling.

questions.question: A trigger runs a SOQL query once for every record in the batch. Why does this design break under a large data load?
options: Query cost scales with record count while the budget does not.
Each query resets the transaction budget for the next one, so cost stays flat.
The row limit is reached long before the statement limit is reached.
Queries issued inside a trigger each consume an extra DML statement.
questions.explanation: A per-record query makes resource use grow with the batch size while the transaction budget stays fixed; binding the whole collection in one query keeps cost proportional to distinct objects touched.

questions.question: A single DML operation inserts 1,000 records and fires a trigger on that object. How often does the trigger code execute?
options: Once per record, each one running with a full transaction budget.
Once per batch of 200 records, each firing as its own transaction.
Once for the entire load, because one DML statement is one transaction.
Twice, once before the database write and once after the commit.
questions.explanation: Triggers run on batches of 200 records, so a larger load fires the trigger several times, and each firing is a fresh transaction with its own governor budget.

questions.question: An object has four separate triggers, each querying the same related records. What is the problem and the recommended fix?
options: Each trigger keeps its own governor budget, so separating them improves isolation.
All logic should move into the trigger file so that nothing is shared across files.
They share one budget and fire unordered; use one trigger per object that routes to a handler.
Multiple triggers are safe whenever each one stays short, readable, and clearly named for its purpose.
questions.explanation: Multiple triggers on one object draw from the same budget and have no guaranteed firing order; a single thin trigger per object that delegates restores ordered execution and predictable budget use.
